analysis.one_liner: Requires agencies to repeal two existing rules for every new one and cap total regulatory costs at zero.
analysis.headline: The bill, which drew no cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would turn a Trump-era executive order into permanent law. Every time a federal agency issues a new rule, it would have to identify at least two existing rules to repeal, and across each year the total added cost of its new rules would have to be zero unless the Office of Management and Budget approved otherwise. Rules for the military, national security, foreign affairs, and agency management would be exempt, and the OMB Director would decide waivers, exceptions, and which rules count. The bill was referred to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that face federal regulation — energy, manufacturing, financial, and other firms with compliance costs — would benefit most. A hard cap on total regulatory cost means that whenever an agency wants to issue a new protection, it must first eliminate old ones, steadily shrinking the stock of rules on pollution, workplace safety, consumer finance, food safety, and more. Because the cap is a dollar cap on costs, rules whose benefits exceed their costs could still be blocked if their costs aren't offset.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each agency to repeal at least two existing rules whenever it issues a new one, and to offset the added cost of new rules so total incremental regulatory cost is no greater than zero each fiscal year [S2][S3].

Gives the OMB Director the authority to set cost allowances for each agency, approve exceptions in writing, and exempt additional categories of rules beyond the military, national security, foreign affairs, and agency-management exemptions [S2][S3].
Bars agencies from issuing any rule that was not included on the most recent Unified Regulatory Agenda unless the OMB Director approves it in advance in writing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules would bear the cost. Fewer and weaker rules mean more exposure to polluted air and water, unsafe workplaces, risky financial products, and unsafe products — harms that are diffuse and often slow to appear, while the compliance savings go to specific companies. The bill also states it creates no enforceable rights, so people harmed by a skipped or repealed rule could not sue over it [S3].

drawbacks.text: A genuine burden exists on the other side: federal compliance costs fall heavily on smaller businesses, and some rules are outdated or duplicative; a supporter would argue a cap forces agencies to prioritize and prune the rulebook [S2][S3].

The bill counts rules and dollars, not benefits. A rule preventing millions of dollars of asthma cases or fraud losses counts only as a cost to be offset, so protections whose benefits far exceed their costs could still be blocked — and the OMB Director's broad waiver and exemption authority concentrates the decision in one political appointee [S3].
The bill explicitly creates no substantive or procedural right enforceable in court, so the public would have no legal recourse if an agency used the cap to shelve a required protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to regulated firms are real but one-sided: the bill prices only the cost of rules, never their benefits, and hard-codes a shrinking rulebook regardless of what a rule protects. Whether the trade is worth it depends entirely on which rules get repealed, and the bill hands that judgment to OMB with no role for the public. It is a blunt tool that would help industries with compliance costs while quietly weakening protections whose value shows up as avoided harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Luke Messer introduced the bill on November 8, 2017, to write Executive Order 13771 — the two-for-one rule repeal and zero-cost regulatory budget — into federal law [S1][S3].

It was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary Committees on the day of introduction, and in December 2017 to the Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S5][S1].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

Because the two-for-one policy already operated as a presidential executive order, the bill's failure left it as an order a later president could simply revoke, rather than a permanent statute an agency and OMB would have had to follow regardless of who held the White House [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who depend on federal protections kept the existing rulebook, and the offset-and-cap scheme stayed an executive order that could be reversed rather than permanent law. The regulated industries that would have gained a statutory cap did not get one.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, finance, and other compliance-cost payers)
industries.note: A two-for-one repeal mandate and a zero-cost cap would steadily shrink federal rules, cutting compliance expenses for firms. The public's cost is weaker protections — more pollution, unsafe workplaces, and risky financial products — so the industry's gain runs against ordinary people's interest.

Agencies would lose discretion: every new rule needs two repeals and a cost offset, and rules off the Unified Regulatory Agenda could not be issued without OMB's written approval. Some agencies might welcome forced prioritization, but the mechanism favors repealing rules over issuing them.

OMB's Director would become the gatekeeper of the entire federal rulebook — setting each agency's cost allowance, approving exceptions, and granting exemptions for additional rule categories. That power is exercised on behalf of the administration's cost priorities, not the public's.
